EXECUTIVE ABSTRACT

The exponential expansion of scientific literature—exceeding two million publications annually across open repositories—has created severe cognitive bottlenecks in academic search, multi-disciplinary exploration, and evidence synthesis. Conventional search platforms suffer from "semantic blindness," relying on sparse lexical matching (BM25/TF-IDF) that fails when queries and papers utilize divergent terminology. Concurrently, generative large language models (LLMs) hallucinate ungrounded assertions and invent non-existent citations. Furthermore, standard machine learning benchmarks commit severe temporal data leakage by evaluating randomized $k$-fold cross-validation on non-stationary literature.

This project report presents Research Copilot, an end-to-end artificial intelligence system engineered for hybrid information retrieval, multi-disciplinary visual navigation, and verified cited question answering over 16,417 arXiv research papers across 35 Computer Science disciplines (2020–2026). The system integrates a two-stage hybrid retrieval engine—fusing sparse BM25 Okapi with dense 384-dimensional FAISS HNSW vectors via Reciprocal Rank Fusion ($k=60$)—and re-ranks top candidates using a deep cross-encoder (ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2). To optimize domain representation, contrastive in-domain fine-tuning is conducted on 14,629 training triplets using Multiple Negatives Ranking Loss (MNRL) paired with an automated false-negative exclusion radius.

Evaluated under strict chronological date boundaries (Train $\\le$ April 2026, Validation May–July 2026, Holdout Test August–October 2026), contrastive fine-tuning achieves statistically significant in-domain retrieval gains on the unseen holdout ($p < 0.0001$): Recall@10 rises from 93.93% to 98.31% (+4.38%), MRR@10 increases from 0.8299 to 0.9338 (+0.1039), and nDCG@10 rises from 0.8564 to 0.9460 (+0.0896), while preserving zero-shot generalization on the external BEIR SciFact benchmark (0.6359 nDCG@10, $p = 0.3290$). On the 35-class categorization ladder, we expose that temporal leakage inflates randomized 5-fold CV by +2.27% to +4.70%, and demonstrate via Holm-Bonferroni corrected hypothesis testing that simple linear classifiers (Linear SVM: 63.60%; Logistic Regression: 64.61%, Brier Score 0.501) match deep neural architectures within statistical sampling margins ($p \ge 0.05$). Multi-label threshold optimization elevates Micro-F1 to 0.6387 (+5.35%) and reduces Hamming loss to 0.0586. The complete framework is deployed as a sub-220 ms FastAPI web service featuring interactive 2D UMAP navigation and sentence-level citation grounding checks.

CHAPTER 1: ACADEMIC SEARCH PROBLEM DOMAIN, RETRIEVAL CONTEXT, AND SYSTEM OBJECTIVES
1.1 Exponential Growth of Scientific Literature and Semantic Blindness

The modern scientific enterprise publishes thousands of peer-reviewed articles and preprints every single day. On arXiv alone, hundreds of new manuscripts in Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence are submitted daily across 40 specialized categories. For researchers, students, and research laboratories, conducting an exhaustive, high-precision literature review has become an overwhelming challenge.

Traditional academic search engines (Google Scholar, PubMed, IEEE Xplore, Semantic Scholar) rely predominantly on inverted indices, keyword tokenization, and lexical scoring functions such as BM25 Okapi and Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF). While lexical algorithms excel at matching exact strings, author names, and acronyms, they exhibit fundamental semantic blindness: they cannot understand contextual meaning, synonyms, or conceptual equivalents. If an author writes about "self-supervised visual representation learning" and a user queries "contrastive image pre-training," pure lexical matching returns poor relevance scores despite near-identical underlying concepts.

1.2 Diagnostic Bottlenecks in Scholarly Discovery: Hallucination and Flat Lists

To bypass the limitations of keyword matching, researchers have increasingly turned to generative Large Language Models (LLMs). However, generative AI introduces severe failure modes in scholarly workflows:

  • Hallucinatory Attribution: LLMs autoregressively synthesize fluent, persuasive paragraphs that cite non-existent papers, hallucinate fictitious author names, and attribute real findings to the wrong manuscripts.
  • Lack of Spatial Overview: Standard interfaces present query results as flat lists of titles. Researchers cannot see how fields overlap, identify neighboring sub-disciplines, or track the historical evolution of research trends across time.
  • Evaluation Deception via Temporal Leakage: In scientific literature analysis, researchers routinely evaluate machine learning models using randomized $k$-fold cross-validation. This shuffles papers from future years (2025–2026) into training sets, allowing classifiers to memorize emerging terminology and falsely inflating performance metrics by +2.3% to +4.7%.
1.3 Quantitative Motivation: Latency, Memory Footprint, and Leakage Prevention

To overcome these challenges, an effective academic research assistant must meet three quantitative engineering benchmarks:

  1. Sub-Second Hybrid Search Latency: Combine lexical BM25 matching and dense vector similarity on CPU hardware, executing under 25 ms without requiring expensive GPU inference servers.
  2. Verified In-Domain Contrastive Fine-Tuning: Fine-tune dense neural embeddings to align scientific titles with abstract representations, raising Recall@10 above 98% while preserving zero-shot generalization on external benchmarks.
  3. Strict Chronological Date-Boundary Discipline: Evaluate all models on strictly forward-looking temporal splits (Train $\\le$ April 2026, Val May–July 2026, Test Aug–Oct 2026) to reflect true production deployment on unseen future preprints.

CHAPTER 2: LITERATURE SURVEY AND COMPARATIVE GAP ANALYSIS
2.1 Evolution of Scientific Information Retrieval and Text Categorization

Computational literature retrieval and document classification have transitioned through three major technological paradigms:

  1. Lexical Inverted Indices (1970s–2010s): Classical models based on TF-IDF weighting and Robertson's BM25 probabilistic framework. While robust and computationally lightweight, lexical systems evaluate superficial character overlap rather than semantic equivalence.
  2. Static & Contextual Distributed Representations (2013–2019): Dense vector embeddings initiated by Word2Vec and GloVe, later superseded by contextual masked language models such as BERT, RoBERTa, and SciBERT. While SciBERT demonstrated the benefit of scientific vocabulary adaptation, utilizing full BERT encoders for real-time document search is computationally prohibitive ($O(N)$ transformer forward passes per query).
  3. Dual-Encoder Dense Retrieval & Hybrid Reranking (2019–Present): Sentence-BERT (Reimers & Gurevych, 2019) introduced Siamese bi-encoders producing fixed-dimensional dense embeddings for vector databases (FAISS). Recent advances demonstrate that combining sparse BM25 and dense bi-encoders via Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), followed by deep cross-encoder re-ranking, yields state-of-the-art retrieval accuracy.

2.3 Benchmark Accuracy Synthesis and Five Unresolved Research Gaps

A systematic synthesis across the surveyed literature reveals five unresolved research gaps that limit real-world academic discovery systems:

  • Gap 1: Temporal Data Leakage in Academic Benchmarking: Prior studies use randomized $k$-fold cross-validation on non-stationary scientific literature, allowing models to cheat by memorizing future terms.
  • Gap 2: False-Negative Penalization in Contrastive Learning: Standard in-batch negative mining assumes all non-target documents are negative. In dense academic clusters, top nearest neighbors are frequently valid synonyms or related work, corrupting gradient updates.
  • Gap 3: Isolated Sparse vs Dense Retrieval: Systems deploy either pure BM25 or pure vector search, failing to harness their complementary strengths on exact acronyms versus conceptual paraphrases.
  • Gap 4: Probability Miscalibration and Deceptive Metrics: Multi-class and multi-label classifiers report raw accuracy or deceptive Hamming loss without evaluating Expected Calibration Error (ECE) or multi-class Brier score.
  • Gap 5: Ungrounded Generative Answers: Existing LLM search tools synthesize paragraphs without verifying whether individual claims are actually entailed by cited source papers.

CHAPTER 3: DATASET COHORTS, TEMPORAL GATEKEEPING, AND PREPROCESSING PIPELINE
3.1 Primary Corpus Benchmark: 16,417 arXiv Papers and Strict Date Boundaries

The core benchmark powering Research Copilot comprises 16,417 computer science research papers spanning January 2020 through October 2026. The dataset is ingested from two complementary sources:

  • Historical OAI Snapshot (5,046 papers): Sourced from the Cornell University arXiv metadata dump, sampled uniformly at 115 papers per month across 2020-01 through 2023-08.
  • Live arXiv REST API (11,371 papers): Ingested directly from export.arxiv.org/api/query at a target rate of 300 papers per month across 2023-09 through 2026-10 using custom rate-limit buffering.
Figure 3.1: Continuous monthly paper sampling volume across all 82 calendar months (January 2020 through October 2026), verifying balanced temporal coverage without month-boundary clustering.
3.2 The OpenAlex Label-Quality Audit: 19% Failure and 100% Genuine arXiv Taxonomy

During preliminary system design, an automated concept expansion pipeline was tested using the OpenAlex API to enrich paper categories. To verify label fidelity, an automated audit was conducted on a random sample of 100 papers, comparing OpenAlex automated tags against genuine author-assigned arXiv primary categories.

The audit revealed that OpenAlex concept tags agreed with author classifications on only 19 out of 100 papers (19.0% accuracy). OpenAlex models exhibited severe concept hallucination—tagging theoretical cryptography preprints with biomedical "Clinical Trial" labels due to words like "test" and "control." Consequently, OpenAlex concepts were completely eliminated. The entire 16,417-paper corpus is indexed using 100% genuine author-submitted arXiv categories (`VALID_CS`, 35 active classes after dropping 4 rare classes with fewer than 20 training instances).

Figure 3.2: Publication distribution across all 35 active Computer Science categories in the 16,417-paper corpus, illustrating heavy representation in Machine Learning (`cs.LG`), Computer Vision (`cs.CV`), and NLP (`cs.CL`).
3.3 Text Length Distributions & Sparse Multi-Label Matrix Topology

Text statistics computed over the full 16,417 corpus reveal:

  • Abstract Character Length: Minimum: 133 chars; Maximum: 2,776 chars; Mean: 1,272.2 chars; Median: 1,273.0 chars; Std: 334.9 chars.
  • Abstract Word Length: Minimum: 15 words; Maximum: 365 words; Mean: 176.1 words; Median: 175.0 words; Std: 46.5 words.
  • Multi-Label Sparsity: Total label assignments across all papers = 34,660. The multi-label indicator matrix (16,417 papers $\times$ 35 categories = 574,595 binary cells) contains 539,935 zero cells, yielding an extreme matrix sparsity of 93.97%.
3.4 Preprocessing and Feature Representations

For every manuscript, text is standardized by concatenating the title and abstract:

text_i = Title_i \cdot \text{". "} \cdot Abstract_i (3.1)

Two distinct feature spaces are extracted for comparative benchmarking:

  1. High-Dimensional Sparse Lexical Space: Extracted using TfidfVectorizer(max_features=30000, ngram_range=(1,2), sublinear_tf=True, stop_words="english").
  2. Dense Semantic Representation Space: Encoded using all-MiniLM-L6-v2 into $\mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^{384}$, normalized to the $L_2$ unit sphere:
    \hat{\mathbf{v}} = \frac{\mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{v}\|_2}, \quad \text{such that } \|\hat{\mathbf{v}}\|_2 = 1 (3.2)

CHAPTER 4: DUAL-PARADIGM MACHINE LEARNING AND RETRIEVAL ARCHITECTURE
4.1 Four-Stage System Workflow and Layered Topology

Research Copilot is organized into four sequential operational stages:

  1. Stage 1 (Ingestion & Preprocessing): Continuous harvesting, text concatenation, and $L_2$ vector normalization.
  2. Stage 2 (Hybrid Candidate Generation): Sparse BM25 scoring and FAISS HNSW dense search returning top 50 candidates each, fused via Reciprocal Rank Fusion into top 30 candidates.
  3. Stage 3 (Cross-Attention Re-Ranking): Full transformer cross-encoder scoring of top 30 candidates into top 8 verified papers.
  4. Stage 4 (Synthesis & Citation Grounding): MMR extractive answer generation, inline numerical citations, and sentence-level grounding verification.
Figure 4.1: Production user interface of Research Copilot displaying the 16,417-paper interactive 2D UMAP canvas, topic clusters, search controls, and live metadata inspection drawer.
4.2 Two-Stage Hybrid Retrieval Branch: BM25, FAISS HNSW, and RRF

For any query $Q$, BM25 computes sparse lexical relevance over term frequencies:

\text{Score}_{\text{BM25}}(D, Q) = \sum_{q \in Q} \text{IDF}(q) \cdot \frac{f(q, D) \cdot (k_1 + 1)}{f(q, D) + k_1 \cdot \left(1 - b + b \cdot \frac{|D|}{\text{avgdl}}\right)} (4.1)

Simultaneously, FAISS HNSW executes approximate nearest-neighbor search in $O(\log N)$ time:

\text{Sim}_{\text{Dense}}(Q, D) = \hat{\mathbf{q}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{d}} = \cos(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{d}) (4.2)

Because BM25 scores are unbounded $[0, \infty)$ and cosine scores are $[-1, 1]$, naive addition requires fragile scaling weights. Instead, Reciprocal Rank Fusion fuses candidates purely by ordinal ranking:

\text{RRF Score}(d) = \sum_{m \in \{\text{Dense}, \text{Sparse}\}} \frac{1}{k + r_m(d)}, \quad \text{with } k = 60 (4.3)
4.3 Deep Cross-Encoder Re-Ranking Branch

While bi-encoders process query and document independently, the Cross-Encoder (cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2) passes the query and candidate title-abstract together through 6 cross-attention layers:

S_{\text{CE}}(Q, D) = \text{Linear}\left( \text{BERT}\left( \text{[CLS]} \circ Q \circ \text{[SEP]} \circ D \circ \text{[SEP]} \right) \right) (4.4)

This computes direct token-to-token cross-attention, re-scoring the top 30 candidates to select the final top 8 papers.

4.4 Contrastive Representation Learning Branch: In-Domain Fine-Tuning

To specialize the general all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embedder to scientific terminology, contrastive fine-tuning is executed using Multiple Negatives Ranking Loss (MNRL):

\mathcal{L}_{\text{MNRL}} = -\frac{1}{B} \sum_{i=1}^B \log \frac{e^{\tau \cdot \cos(\mathbf{q}_i, \mathbf{d}_i^+)}}{e^{\tau \cdot \cos(\mathbf{q}_i, \mathbf{d}_i^+)} + \sum_{j \neq i} e^{\tau \cdot \cos(\mathbf{q}_i, \mathbf{d}_j^+)} + \sum_{k} e^{\tau \cdot \cos(\mathbf{q}_i, \mathbf{d}_{i,k}^-)}} (4.5)

False Negative Exclusion Radius: Mining hard negatives strictly by topic cluster risks selecting abstracts that are near-identical to the query title. An exclusion radius in train_embedder.py removes the top 5 nearest neighbors of the positive abstract from ever being chosen as hard negatives.

5.1 Decoupled Python and FastAPI Software Stack

5.2 Extractive MMR Synthesis and Sentence-Level Citation Grounding Check

To guarantee zero hallucinatory claims in the "Ask" mode, Research Copilot deploys Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR) extractive synthesis. For each candidate sentence $s_i$ in the top retrieved abstracts:

\text{MMR} = \arg\max_{s_i \in C \setminus S} \left[ \lambda \cdot \cos(\mathbf{s}_i, \mathbf{q}) - (1 - \lambda) \cdot \max_{s_j \in S} \cos(\mathbf{s}_i, \mathbf{s}_j) \right], \quad \lambda = 0.7 (5.1)

Every extracted claim is tagged with an inline numerical badge [n] linking to source abstract $n$. The grounding verification algorithm encodes claim sentence $s$ and all sentences of cited abstract $D_n$. If $\max \cos(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{d}) \ge 0.45$, the claim is verified (`✓`); otherwise, it is flagged with a warning (`⚠`).

5.3 Confidence Gatekeeping and Out-of-Domain Refusal Protocol

When presented with queries outside Computer Science (e.g., baking recipes or clinical surgeries), generative systems invent plausible sounding falsehoods. Research Copilot enforces an explicit score-based refusal gatekeeper:

\text{Refuse}(Q) = \mathbf{1}\left( \max_{d \in \text{Hits}} S_{\text{CE}}(Q, d) < -5.0 \right) (5.2)

If the maximum cross-encoder score is below $-5.0$, the server returns {"answer": "", "confident": false}, protecting users from ungrounded responses.

6.5 Production Case Studies, Grounding Verification, and Safety Guardrails

To demonstrate the end-to-end functionality, academic veracity, and ethical failure handling of Research Copilot in production, the subsequent diagnostic case cards summarize six real operational queries executed against the live system. Every generated claim undergoes sentence-level cosine grounding verification against the retrieved arXiv abstracts to enforce academic transparency.

Case Study 1: Multi-Document Graph Neural Network Query 100% Verified Grounding
Query: "Contrastive learning for graph neural networks"
Top Retrieved Paper: Cross-view Self-Supervised Learning on Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network via Bootstrapping (arXiv: cs.LG)
Synthesized Answer: "In this paper, we propose the novel Label Contrastive Coding based Graph Neural Network (LCGNN) to utilize label information more effectively and comprehensively. [2] A crucial step in contrastive learning is the creation of 'augmented' graphs from the input graphs. [4] A large number of graph contrastive learning approaches have shown promising performance for representation learning on graphs, which train models by maximizing agreement between original graphs and their augmented views (i.e., positive views). [6]"
Grounding Verification: 4 sentences evaluated; 4/4 verified supported against primary source abstracts ($s_{\text{cos}} \ge 0.67$); 100% attribution precision with direct arXiv links.
Case Study 2: Generative Vision & Text-to-Image Synthesis 100% Verified Grounding
Query: "Diffusion models for high resolution image synthesis"
Top Retrieved Paper: Layered Diffusion Model for One-Shot High Resolution Text-to-Image Synthesis (arXiv: cs.CV)
Synthesized Answer: "We demonstrate that higher resolution synthesis can be achieved by layering convolutions at additional resolution scales, in contrast to other methods which require additional models for super-resolution synthesis. [1] Diffusion models (DMs) have recently gained attention with state-of-the-art performance in text-to-image synthesis. [2] Current large-scale diffusion models represent a giant leap forward in conditional image synthesis, capable of interpreting diverse cues like text, human poses, and edges. [6]"
Grounding Verification: 4 sentences evaluated; 4/4 verified supported against source abstracts ($s_{\text{cos}} \ge 0.58$); exact algorithmic references verified.
Case Study 3: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (LoRA) 100% Verified Grounding
Query: "Parameter efficient fine tuning LoRA"
Top Retrieved Paper: GeoLoRA: Geometric integration for parameter efficient fine-tuning (arXiv: cs.LG)
Synthesized Answer: "Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has become a widely used method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large-scale, pre-trained neural networks. [1] However, LoRA and its extensions face several challenges, including the need for rank adaptivity, robustness, and computational efficiency during the fine-tuning process. [1] Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) approaches have emerged as a viable alternative by allowing us to fine-tune models by updating only a small number of parameters. [2]"
Grounding Verification: 4 sentences evaluated; 4/4 verified supported ($s_{\text{cos}} \ge 0.46$, max $1.00$); zero factual drift.
Case Study 4: Federated Learning & Privacy Safeguards 100% Verified Grounding
Query: "Federated learning differential privacy"
Top Retrieved Paper: Evaluation of Differential Privacy Mechanisms on Federated Learning (arXiv: cs.CR)
Synthesized Answer: "Differential privacy is one of the methods to solve the problem of privacy protection in federated learning. [2] Therefore, we proposed an adaptive differential privacy method based on federated learning. [2] This paper presents a gradient leakage resilient approach to privacy-preserving federated learning with per training example-based client differential privacy, coined as Fed-CDP. [6]"
Grounding Verification: 4 sentences evaluated; 4/4 verified supported ($s_{\text{cos}} \ge 0.70$); all cryptographic definitions confirmed.
Case Study 5: Automated Out-of-Domain Refusal Gate (Safety & Anti-Hallucination) AUTOMATED REFUSAL TRIGGERED
Adversarial / Nonsense Query: "quantum teleportation recipe for baking banana bread in hypergravity"
Top Candidate Paper Found: Multimarked Spatial Search by Continuous-Time Quantum Walk (arXiv: cs.DS)
Cross-Encoder Relevance Score: -10.7906 (System Refusal Threshold: $\\tau_{\text{refuse}} = -5.0$)
Engine Decision & Response: Score (-10.7906) < Threshold (-5.0) → "Refused (no confident papers found)"
Safety Analysis: Rather than forcing generative completion or fabricating culinary recipes with spurious physics citations, the automated cross-encoder refusal threshold cleanly terminates generation. This guarantees zero hallucination risk on out-of-distribution inputs.
Case Study 6: Cross-Domain Polysemy & Vocabulary Boundary Failure Analysis BOUNDARY AMBIGUITY IDENTIFIED
Domain Stress Query: "Transformers in electric power transmission networks"
Top Retrieved Paper: Moving Target Defense for Robust Monitoring of Electric Grid Transformers in Adversarial Environments (arXiv: cs.GT)
Cross-Encoder Relevance Score: 0.3402 (Low confidence margin)
Sentence Grounding Check: 0 of 4 sentences supported against retrieved abstracts ($s_{\text{cos}} \le 0.27$); system flagged claims with warning icons (`⚠`).
Failure Diagnosis & Academic Insight: The query exhibits severe cross-disciplinary polysemy. The user sought electrical power engineering literature on physical electromagnetic step-up/step-down transformers in high-voltage grids. Because the corpus is constrained to 35 Computer Science disciplines, the retrieval engine matched papers applying deep learning "Transformer" attention models to power grid sensor data. The automated grounding check correctly alerted the user to the semantic divergence.

CHAPTER 7: CONCLUSIONS, ETHICAL CONSIDERATIONS, AND FUTURE ENHANCEMENTS
7.1 Synthesis of Experimental Findings and Engineering Takeaways

This project successfully designed, implemented, and benchmarked Research Copilot, establishing four key scientific and engineering conclusions:

  1. Strict Chronological Splits Eliminate Leakage: Enforcing date-boundary evaluation exposes that standard randomized 5-fold cross-validation inflates classification accuracy by +2.27% to +4.70% through temporal term leakage.
  2. In-Domain Contrastive Tuning Yields Substantial Retrieval Gains: Training all-MiniLM-L6-v2 with MNRL and a 5-NN exclusion radius achieves +4.38% Recall@10 and +0.1039 MRR@10 gains ($p < 0.0001$) while preserving zero-shot generalization on BEIR SciFact ($p = 0.3290$).
  3. Linear Models Match Deep Architectures: After Holm-Bonferroni correction, simple well-calibrated linear classifiers (Linear SVM: 63.60%; Logistic Regression: 64.61%, Brier Score 0.501) perform equivalently to deep neural networks ($p \ge 0.05$) while training 10x faster.
  4. Threshold Tuning Mitigates Multi-Label Sparsity: Optimizing per-label decision thresholds on validation data raises Micro-F1 from 0.5852 to 0.6387 (+5.35%) and lowers Hamming loss to 0.0586.
7.2 Academic Integrity Safeguards and Hallucination Prevention

In alignment with ethical AI principles, Research Copilot enforces strict safeguards:

  • Every factual claim requires an inline numerical citation linking directly to its underlying arXiv abstract.
  • Sentence-level cosine grounding checks flag unsupported sentences with warning icons (`⚠`).
  • Out-of-domain queries triggering cross-encoder scores below $-5.0$ are automatically refused rather than hallucinated.
7.3 Future Research Directions
  • Natural Language Inference (NLI) Grounding: Replace cosine grounding checks with formal cross-encoder entailment models classifying claims into Entailment, Neutral, or Contradiction.
  • Comparative Topic Coherence Study: Conduct empirical comparisons between HDBSCAN/c-TF-IDF topic modeling and Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) evaluated via $C_v$ coherence.
  • Autoregressive Trend Forecasting: Implement vector autoregressive time-series models over the 82-month dataset to project emerging research trajectories.
  • Full-Text PDF Ingestion: Extend indexing beyond abstracts to full PDF manuscripts, mathematical equations, and benchmark tables.
